clue.text: Defence of royal retainer in speech

indicators.note: something said in speech is heard rather than read, so the clue wants a sound match

blocks.note: a royal retainer is an aide who serves at the palace

explanation.surface: Someone praises how a loyal courtier spoke up for the monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: Said aloud, PALACE AIDE runs together into PALISADE.
explanation.definitionFit: A palisade is a fence of pointed wooden stakes built as a fortification against attack.

clue.text: Fair start from Tories in charge

indicators.note: the start from a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept
one piece sits in another, so it is placed inside the second

blocks.note: first part of a fee, a charge for a service
the opening letter of Tories
the end of a fee, a charge

explanation.surface: A political report on the Conservatives taking over the running of a village fair.
explanation.walkthrough: FEE, a charge, takes T inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A fete is an outdoor gathering with stalls and games, much the same thing as a fair or carnival.

indicators.note: one piece placed in another means it goes inside the second

blocks.note: first letter of FEN, a bog
everybody is all
rest of FEN, low marshy land

explanation.surface: A disreputable person and their whole crowd end up stuck in a marsh.
explanation.walkthrough: A fen is a flat wet marsh, as in the English Fens of East Anglia.
explanation.definitionFit: Fallen describes someone morally ruined or corrupted, the same idea as degenerate used as an adjective.

clue.text: Leave more bitter about sweetheart, upset

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its centre, so only the middle letter is wanted
about means going round, so one piece wraps around the other
in a down clue, upset turns the whole thing upside down, so it reads backwards

blocks.note: more bitter in taste is tarter
the middle letter of sweet, its heart

explanation.surface: Someone told to go away after souring on a lover who has been left distressed.
explanation.walkthrough: TARTER takes E inside to make TAERTER, which read upwards gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To retreat is to withdraw or pull back from a place, which is a way of departing from it.

blocks.note: surface reading: Hamlet's famous line musing on death and what dreams may come
setter's reading: 'to sleep' and 'to dream' are both examples of a verb form preceded by 'to'

explanation.walkthrough: The quotation is from Hamlet's 'To be or not to be' speech; the question mark flags that it is being read as grammar, not poetry.
explanation.definitionFit: The infinitive is the basic verb form, which in English is usually introduced by the particle 'to'.

indicators.note: one thing including another holds it within, so the second piece goes inside

blocks.note: first part of LOG, a written record
to trespass in the biblical sense is to sin
end of LOG

explanation.surface: A trespasser loses the logbook that would have recorded their intrusion.
explanation.definitionFit: Losing something means misplacing it so it cannot be found, which is what mislaying describes.

clue.text: Labour’s leader with brilliant tax cut

indicators.note: the leader of a word is the letter at its front, so only that is kept

blocks.note: the first letter of Labour
ace means excellent or brilliant
a rate is a local tax

explanation.surface: A political headline: the Labour leader's excellent plan to reduce taxation.
explanation.walkthrough: Rates were the old British local property tax.
explanation.definitionFit: To lacerate is to tear or gash the flesh, a deep wound of the kind a cut makes.

blocks.note: to desire is to want
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O
N is the abbreviation for noon

explanation.surface: A lusty urge for a romantic tryst before midday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'before' simply orders the pieces: O comes ahead of N.
explanation.definitionFit: Wanton describes someone sexually unrestrained or promiscuous, close in sense to lustful.

blocks.note: W is the standard abbreviation for with
an inning is a team's or batter's turn at the crease in baseball or cricket

explanation.surface: A cricket or baseball player looks forward to their go at the crease.
explanation.definitionFit: A winning smile or manner is charming and attractive, so winning works as a synonym for engaging.

indicators.note: something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so the clue wants a word that sounds the same

blocks.note: to raise something is to put it higher

explanation.surface: News that a landlord is putting up the rent.
explanation.definitionFit: To hire a thing is to pay for its temporary use, the same as renting it.

clue.text: An impediment to freedom of speech?

definitions.text: An impediment to freedom of speech?

blocks.clueFragment: An impediment to freedom of speech?
blocks.note: surface reading: censorship or a law that silences people

blocks.clueFragment: An impediment to freedom of speech?
blocks.note: setter's reading: a throat inflammation that physically stops you talking freely

explanation.walkthrough: 'Freedom of speech' points at politics; the question mark hints it is literal, the ability to talk at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Laryngitis is inflammation of the voice box which makes a person hoarse or unable to talk.

blocks.note: a dam is a barrier holding back water
a pen is an enclosure, a compound for animals

explanation.surface: Inspect the fence around a fortified site.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' would mean above; in this across clue it simply joins the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To dampen enthusiasm or spirits is to restrain or curb it, one sense of check.

indicators.note: pocketing something means putting it away inside, so it is held within

blocks.note: first part of PRIED, meddled or interfered
vile means foul or filthy
G is short for grand, a thousand pounds
end of PRIED

explanation.surface: A wealthy meddler quietly siphons off a dirty thousand.
explanation.walkthrough: PRIED wraps around VILE plus G.
explanation.definitionFit: Privileged people enjoy special advantages from wealth and status, so the word is used loosely for well-off.

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter, so only that is taken
around means surrounding, so one piece goes round the other

blocks.note: first letter of AIDING, helping
the first letter of bank
rest of AIDING

explanation.surface: A company assists with the launch of a new bank.
explanation.definitionFit: Abiding means lasting and steadfast, as in an abiding friendship, close in sense to firm or enduring.

indicators.note: being seen in something places it inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: first part of DEED, an action
CID is the Criminal Investigation Department, British plain-clothes detectives
end of DEED

explanation.surface: Determined police officers are spotted on the job.
explanation.definitionFit: A decided person is firm and unwavering in their views, which is what resolute means.

clue.text: Resolve without proposal to keep single

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: ex means without, as in ex dividend
first part of PLAN, a proposal
I is the Roman numeral one, a single
end of PLAN

explanation.surface: A bachelor's decision to stay single without ever popping the question.
explanation.definitionFit: To explain a mystery is to clear it up, which is one sense of resolve, as in resolving a puzzle.

clue.text: Touching when snatching win before time

indicators.note: snatching something means grabbing hold of it, so it ends up held inside

blocks.note: first letter of AS, when
to win something is to gain it
end of AS
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A moving sporting moment, clinching victory just as the clock runs out.
explanation.definitionFit: Something leaning against a wall is in contact with it, so against can mean in physical contact.

clue.text: Fantastic being clothed in chaster lingerie

indicators.note: being clothed in something means being covered by it, so the word lies within the letters

blocks.note: runs across the two words

explanation.surface: Someone looks marvellous dressed in modest underwear.
explanation.definitionFit: Sterling as an adjective means of excellent quality, as in sterling work, close to fantastic.

indicators.note: something eating another takes it inside, so one piece goes within

blocks.note: first letter of PEST, a pain or nuisance
rhubarb is British slang for nonsense, as is rot
rest of PEST

explanation.surface: A complaint about stomach ache after eating rhubarb.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain rhubarb is also slang for nonsense or meaningless chatter.
explanation.definitionFit: To protest is to complain or object, which is what a gripe expresses.

blocks.note: first meaning: the captain of a vessel
second meaning: a long-snouted sea fish, also called the saury

explanation.surface: A ship's captain lands a catch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head of ship' tempts you to take just S; it is the whole person in charge.
explanation.definitionFit: A skipper is the master of a boat, and also the name of a small slender sea fish.

clue.text: Nation‘s ally swamped by Japanese currency

indicators.note: being swamped by something means being engulfed, so one piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: first letter of SEN, a Japanese coin
to ally is to join or unite, as is to wed
end of SEN

explanation.surface: A country's partner is overwhelmed by the yen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ally' looks like a noun but is the verb, to join; the sen is a hundredth of a yen.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweden is a Scandinavian country, so it is an example of a nation.

clue.text: Pierce middle of blockages blocking drain

indicators.note: the middle of a word is its central letter, so only that is kept
something blocking a pipe lodges inside it, so one piece goes within

blocks.note: first letter of SEWER, a drain
the central letter of blockages
rest of SEWER

explanation.surface: A plumber pokes a rod into the heart of a clogged drain.
explanation.definitionFit: To skewer something is to run a long pin through it, which is the same as piercing it.

clue.text: Classified as somewhat monotonous or tedious

indicators.note: somewhat means partly, so only part of the following words is used

blocks.note: runs across the three words

explanation.surface: Secret papers are labelled rather dull and boring.
explanation.definitionFit: Sorted means arranged into groups or categories, which is what classified means in the filing sense.

clue.text: Supporter with moan about new player

indicators.note: about means going round, so one piece is wrapped around another

blocks.note: first part of BEEF, a moan or complaint
N is the abbreviation for new
end of BEEF
a player on stage is an actor

explanation.surface: A fan grumbles about a newly signed member of the team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supporter' and 'player' suggest football, but beef is slang for a grievance.
explanation.definitionFit: A benefactor gives money or help to a cause or person, so is a backer or patron.

indicators.note: the finish of a word is its final letter, so only that is kept

blocks.note: china means mate in Cockney rhyming slang: china plate rhymes with mate, a pal
the last letter of plate

explanation.surface: A white porcelain dish with a fine glaze.
explanation.walkthrough: 'china plate' reads as a phrase, but china alone is rhyming slang for a friend.
explanation.definitionFit: Pale means light in colour or drained of colour, as a frightened face turns white.

indicators.note: initially points at the first letters of each word before it

blocks.note: the opening letters of those four words

explanation.surface: Kitchen instructions: first strip off the skin.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the instruction and the meaning: peeling is removing the outside.
explanation.definitionFit: To pare fruit is to trim off its skin or outer layer with a knife.

clue.text: Humble of French chap embracing European

indicators.note: to embrace something is to hold it in your arms, so it goes inside

blocks.note: de is French for of
first letter of MAN, a chap
E is the abbreviation for European
end of MAN

explanation.surface: A modest Frenchman hugs a fellow European.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Humble' looks like an adjective but is the verb, to bring low.
explanation.definitionFit: To demean someone is to lower their dignity or status, which is what humbling them does.

indicators.note: putting something into another places it inside

blocks.note: first part of STING, a do or swindle
E is the abbreviation for English
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the Queen
end of STING

explanation.surface: A courtier showing the monarch into a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'do' looks like a party; here it is a swindle, as in to do someone.
explanation.definitionFit: Steering someone means guiding them in a direction, as an usher leads guests to their places.
